Comparison-shape S5 corporate-policy-change event sibling to
uniswap-frontend-delisting-2023 (the canonical L4-only
frontend-delisting anchor). Aave's 2022-08-13 frontend block is
the earliest documented L4 DeFi-frontend compliance action in the
Tornado Cash 2022 cascade family, and the only event in the corpus
that names TRM Labs (rather than Chainalysis) as the screening-API
provider. Paper-relevant because it isolates the same
frontend-operator / protocol-layer split documented under
uniswap-frontend-delisting-2023, but with two distinguishing
features: (a) the trigger is an upstream OFAC SDN action (rather
than the frontend operator's independent compliance judgment), and
(b) the mechanism is an off-the-shelf compliance-screening API
rather than a curated token-list. Together with
infura-alchemy-tornado-rpc-block-2022 (L3) and
circle-usdc-tornado-2022 (asset_onchain), this row completes the
S5_corporate cascade triangle downstream of the 2022-08-08 OFAC
Tornado Cash designation: asset-issuer (Circle, ~6h),
RPC-provider (Infura/Alchemy, ~24h), frontend-operator (Aave,
~120h / 5 days). The 5-day lag relative to the upstream OFAC
trigger (2022-08-08) is paper-relevant for the cascade-latency
comparison and is tracked at the cross-event level (delta_hours
inside this event is 0 because the Aave trigger and the Aave
observation share a day-precision timestamp).

Empirical shape: comparison (1 observed_change layer — L4 frontend
load-bearing). Admission tier: empirical_case (≥1 observed_change
layer with direct attribution). Stratum coding: S5_corporate. The

scoped_knowledge:
This event is the Argentine national-competent-authority
implementation of the FATF R15 2019 VASP travel-rule extension,
arriving ~5 years after FATF R15 and ~10 years after the
earliest Argentine AML-pipeline capture of virtual-currency
operations (Resolución UIF 300/2014). The mechanism is class-

in the 90-day post-publication window is class-level on PSAVs
rather than exchange-specific: the dominant Argentine-market
actors entered the registration pipeline rather than exiting,
consistent with a registry-style compliance instrument rather
than a prohibition. The 2025 supersession by RG 1058/2025
(effective 2025-12-31) is a candidate sibling event for future
authoring.

citation.note:
Boletín Oficial de la República Argentina — publication of
Comisión Nacional de Valores (CNV) Resolución General N°
994/2024 on 2024-03-25, establishing the Registro de
Proveedores de Servicios de Activos Virtuales (PSAV /
Virtual Asset Service Provider Registry). The resolution
implements Ley 27.739 (the AML modernisation law that
amended Ley 25.246) and introduces the PSAV figure into
Argentine financial-supervision law. A PSAV is defined as
any individual or legal entity that, as a business, carries
out one or more of (i) exchange between virtual assets and
legal tender, (ii) exchange between forms of virtual assets,
(iii) transfer of virtual assets, (iv) custody / management
of virtual assets or instruments allowing control over such
assets, and (v) participation in / provision of financial
services related to a virtual-asset offer or sale. All such
providers must register in the PSAV registry before
commencing operations; failure to register results in a ban
on operating in Argentina. The registry is closed to
applicants resident, domiciled, or incorporated in
jurisdictions on the FATF non-cooperative / high-risk list
or in non-cooperative tax-transparency jurisdictions.

**NEW EVENT AUTHORED — DRYRUN 2026-05-17**. Historical-baseline
contextual case for Resolución UIF N° 300/2014 issued 2014-07-04
by Argentina's Unidad de Información Financiera (UIF / Financial
Information Unit), the autonomous AML/CFT authority created by
Law 25.246. The resolution imposed STR/KYC-style reporting
obligations on Article-20 obliged entities (sujetos obligados) —
banks, financial institutions, casas de cambio, broker-dealers,
escribanos, and other AML-regulated counterparties — in respect
of virtual-currency operations, effective 2014-08-01. Authored at
status=draft pending human audit of (i) Infoleg URL reachability
and Wayback snapshot pinning, (ii) the CoinDesk and El Cronista
English/Spanish contextual anchors, and (iii) any exchange-side
evidence of Argentina-resident or obliged-entity-side cutoff that
may exist in contemporaneous press coverage but was not located
in this authoring pass.

Significance: this is the earliest dataset case of a non-US
national regulator imposing AML-style reporting obligations on
obliged entities specifically in respect of virtual-currency
operations — pre-dating the FATF June 2014 "Virtual Currencies:
Key Definitions and Potential AML/CFT Risks" report only by
~3 weeks, and pre-dating FATF Recommendation 15's 2019 extension
to virtual-asset service providers (VASPs) by ~5 years. It is
the contextual precursor to fatf-r15-vasp-travel-rule-2019 in
the AML-style obliged-entity reporting lineage.

scoped_knowledge:
This event is the earliest dataset case of a non-US national
regulator extending AML-style reporting obligations to virtual-
currency operations via obliged-entity channels — pre-dating the
FATF June 2014 key-definitions report by ~3 weeks and the FATF
R15 2019 VASP travel-rule extension by ~5 years. The mechanism
is class-level: Resolución 300/2014 does not name specific
exchanges; instead it leverages the existing Article-20 obliged-
entity register under Law 25.246 to capture virtual-currency
operations within the pre-existing AML reporting pipeline. This
is a meaningful contrast with the China 2013-12 PBOC banking-
rail-severance pattern (which prohibited bank services to
bitcoin) and with the Iceland 2014-03 CBI FX-Act-reuse pattern
(which prohibited Icelandic-resident bitcoin purchases under
capital-controls law): the Argentine UIF chose neither
prohibition nor capital-controls reuse but rather AML-pipeline
capture, which became the dominant FATF-aligned regulatory
pattern globally after 2019. The 2024 supersession by Resolución
49/2024 is a candidate sibling event for future authoring.

target.enumeration_note:
Target is the class of "sujetos obligados" (obliged entities)
enumerated in Article 20 of Law 25.246 — Argentine banks,
financial institutions, exchange houses (casas de cambio),
broker-dealers, escribanos, and other AML-regulated counterparties

citation.note:
Official text of Resolución UIF N° 300/2014 hosted on Infoleg
(servicios.infoleg.gob.ar), the canonical Argentine legal-
information database maintained by the Ministerio de Justicia.
Dated 2014-07-04 and signed by the UIF (Unidad de Información
Financiera / Financial Information Unit), the autonomous AML/CFT
authority created by Law 25.246. The resolution defines
"monedas virtuales" (virtual currencies) as digital
representations of value that function as a medium of exchange,
unit of account, and/or store of value but lack legal-tender
status and are not issued or guaranteed by any state, and it
requires obliged entities (sujetos obligados) enumerated in
Article 20 of Law 25.246 — banks, financial institutions,
exchange houses, broker-dealers, escribanos, and other
AML-regulated counterparties — to report all virtual-currency
operations to the UIF via the agency's online reporting portal.
The provisions took effect on 2014-08-01. Specific Wayback
snapshot timestamp requires re-pinning in human audit before
this citation may serve as an admission anchor.

scoped_knowledge:
Bitcoinica is the pre-Mt-Gox-collapse anchor for operator-led
exchange shutdowns triggered by security incidents rather than
regulatory pressure. The case illustrates the early-era pattern
in which leveraged-bitcoin trading venues, operating without
the cold-storage hygiene, insurance backstops, or regulatory
recovery mechanisms that would later emerge, were closed
unilaterally by their operators after intrusion events outpaced
the platform's solvency reserves. The Bitcoinica shutdown
trajectory — Zhou Tong founds 2011-09, Intersango acquires
operational control early 2012, 2012-03 Linode breach, 2012-05-11
second intrusion and operator-led shutdown, 2012-08-02 formal
liquidation announcement — is conceptually the ancestor of later
CEX-failure cascades (Mt. Gox 2014, FTX 2022, etc.) in which
the offramp_cex surface is removed by operator-initiated closure
rather than by regulator order. As a discovery-ledger event, this
row provides the pre-2013 baseline observation that the
offramp_cex cascade axis is subject to operator-initiated closure
independent of any regulator-named trigger.

CFTC Docket No. 16-19, dated 2016-06-02. Findings: from
approximately April 2013 through at least February 2016 Bitfinex
operated an online platform for exchanging and trading
cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, and offered financed retail
commodity transactions in Bitcoin to U.S. customers without

analysis_notes:
comparison documenting the first-ever OFAC sanction of a virtual currency
mixer. Blender.io was designated 94 days before Tornado Cash and tests whether the Tornado
cascade shape generalizes to the mixer class, or whether Tornado's cross-layer reaction was
driven by Tornado-specific properties (Ethereum native, smart-contract-based, USDC-
interacting).

Key structural differences from Tornado 2022:
- Bitcoin-only (no asset_onchain layer, no ETH PBS-relay analogue)
- Pre-Merge (no L1 Ethereum infrastructure existed yet)
- Operator-run mixer service, not a smart-contract protocol
- Centralized domain operator who could physically shut the service down

The one grounded observation is at L4 frontend: blender.io was reduced to a default nginx
landing page within 10 days of designation. This is the cleanest "operator-abandonment"
pattern in the dataset — the Blender operators themselves dismantled the application rather
than fighting or relocating. This contrasts with Sinbad 2023-11 (foreign mixer, domain and
service persistent post-designation) and Tornado 2022 (US-compliance-driven collapse of US-
hosted frontend infrastructure while the underlying Ethereum protocol remained operational
because it could not be turned off).

Follow-up directions (post-admission): (1) chain-analytics firm report (Chainalysis / TRM Labs / Elliptic)
tagging of Blender-clustered BTC addresses, quantifying CEX deposit blocks; (2) any news
or legal archive for the Blender operators' post-2022 fate.

Bitcoin-only event class currently has no observed_change at L1 / asset / RPC layers because
those layers are structurally not_applicable for Bitcoin. The L4 observed_change alone is
enough to meet comparison's 1-2 changed-layer requirement once the draft is promoted.

analysis_notes:
**NEW EVENT AUTHORED — DRYRUN 2026-05-17**. Phase E follow-on
authoring pass after the 2026-05-16 pre-Bitcoin baseline 2008-2012
lean run. This event populates the historical_baseline_2013_2016
tier with one of the earliest explicit nation-state-level crypto
prohibitions in the global record.

BCB Board Resolution No. 044/2014 (issued 2014-05-06) prohibited
the use within Bolivia of any currency not issued and regulated by
the Bolivian state, explicitly naming bitcoin and a list of other
electronic/virtual currencies. Bolivia in 2014-05 is commonly cited
alongside Thailand 2013-07 (Bank of Thailand verbal prohibition) and
China 2013-12 (PBOC Notice 2013/289) as one of the first three nation-
state crypto-prohibition actions; among these three, the Bolivia
resolution is the most class-level and prospective because Bolivia
in 2014-05 had no domestically-operated bitcoin exchange of
meaningful scale.

Why null_event / null_case / observed_no_change: the prohibition is
class-level and prospective rather than cascade-producing. There is
no clear point-in-time observable cascade in the public record —
no Bolivian crypto exchange ceased operating because none of
meaningful scale existed at the time of issuance — and no
downstream Bolivian-domestic L0/L3/L4/asset_onchain observable
surfaces are engaged by the resolution. The single load-bearing
observation row is observed_no_change at offramp_cex with a
falsifiable scope_descriptor spanning 2014-05-06 to the end of
the historical-baseline tier (2016-12-31).

Why temporal_tier=historical_baseline_2013_2016 and analysis_use=
historical_baseline: events 2013-2016 belong to the
historical_baseline_2013_2016 tier per the project's tiered frame.
analysis_use=historical_baseline (the canonical form, not the
contextual_baseline alias that the codebook §6 explicitly rejects)
excludes this row from the 2017+ comparable-analysis denominator.

Why trigger.type=regulatory_enforcement: per codebook §5.1 (2026-05-17
update), regulatory_enforcement is the canonical trigger.type for
non-US national-regulator administrative actions, including central-
bank prohibition resolutions of this kind. nation_state_block would
be the alternative if Resolution 044/2014 directed ISP / payment-rail
network blocking, but it does not; the BCB action is administrative
monetary-authority prohibition rather than network-layer block.
S4_nation_state is the permitted stratum for regulatory_enforcement
per codebook §5.2.

Why target.kind=entity and enumeration=subset: per codebook §7,
class_level is not a valid enumeration value; class-level regulatory
scope is recorded as subset with the class-level rationale captured
in enumeration_note. target.kind=entity matches sibling treatment
for class-level regulatory predicates (see fincen-virtual-currency-
msb-guidance-2013 and china-pboc-crypto-ban-2013-12).

Why L0/L1/L3/L4/asset_onchain are not_applicable: the Bolivian
prohibition is a monetary-authority class-level instrument that does
not engage network blocking, frontend takedown, stablecoin admin-
freeze, or post-Merge L1/L3 measurement surfaces. construct-out-of-
scope or construct-did-not-exist reasoning applies in each case,
consistent with the sibling china-pboc-crypto-ban-2013-12 treatment
of pre-Merge nation-state banking-rail events.

Cross-event positioning: the canonical 2013-2014 first-touch nation-
state crypto-prohibition sibling set is Thailand 2013-07 (BoT) +
China 2013-12 (PBOC) + Bolivia 2014-05 (BCB). The Thailand event is
not yet authored as a separate YAML; this event's related_events
field forward-references that planned sibling alongside the already-
authored china-pboc-crypto-ban-2013-12.

Origin=agent_draft and status=draft per the agent-authoring
convention. A human reviewer must (a) re-pin the bcb.gob.bo
Resolution 044/2014 PDF Wayback snapshot, (b) re-pin the City A.M.
contemporaneous coverage Wayback snapshot, and (c) decide whether
observed_no_change with the falsifiable 2014-05-06 to 2016-12-31
scope window admits the event as null_case before promoting status
beyond draft.

coverage.note:
BCB Resolution 044/2014 does not direct ISP-level domain blocking
or DNS interference against any crypto-related host. It is a
monetary-authority prohibition on the use of non-state currencies,
not a network-layer block. not_applicable on construct-out-of-
scope grounds, consistent with the sibling china-pboc-crypto-ban-
2013-12 treatment of banking-and-monetary-rail nation-state events.

Bitcoin proof-of-work consensus in 2014-05 has no protocol-level
relay-filter primitive analogous to the post-Merge Ethereum PBS
relay surface that the L1 layer measures. The Ethereum Merge
itself is ~8 years downstream (2022-09-15). not_applicable on
construct-did-not-exist grounds.

The MEV-Boost / Flashbots Protect / MEV-Blocker public-RPC
compliance substrate that the L3 layer measures did not exist
in 2014 (Flashbots Protect launched 2022-11; MEV-Blocker
launched 2023-03-27). not_applicable on construct-did-not-exist
grounds.

Resolution 044/2014 does not require, name, or contemplate any
crypto-related frontend takedown or geo-blocking within Bolivia.
The prohibition attaches to the use of non-state currencies in
Bolivian commerce, not to the public-facing web surface of any
named operator. No Bolivian crypto exchange of meaningful scale
existed in the 2014-05 public record. not_applicable on construct-
out-of-scope grounds.

Bitcoin native asset has no issuer-side blacklist / freeze admin
method. Resolution 044/2014 does not engage a stablecoin-issuer
admin path (USDT first issued ~2014-10; chain-wide admin freezes
arose later). not_applicable on construct-did-not-exist grounds.

The substantive regulatory effect of Resolution 044/2014 is to
bar use of bitcoin and other non-state currencies in Bolivian
commerce. The cascade, however, has no clear point-in-time
offramp / CEX cessation in the public record because Bolivia in
2014-05 had no domestically-operated bitcoin exchange of
meaningful scale: the prohibition is prospective and class-level
rather than triggering an observable in-country exchange
shutdown. Marked not_measured because the load-bearing cascade
is class-level and prospective rather than a single point-in-
time observable CEX cessation; the corresponding observation
row below records this as observed_no_change with a falsifiable
scope window.

citation.note:
Banco Central de Bolivia (BCB) Board Resolution No. 044/2014,
issued 2014-05-06, prohibiting the use within Bolivia of any
currency, coin, or denomination that is not issued and
regulated by the Bolivian state (the boliviano, BOB). The
resolution explicitly names "bitcoin" and a list of other
electronic/virtual currencies (e.g. namecoin, peercoin,
primecoin, feathercoin, quark) and bars their use as a means
of payment, store of value, or unit of account in Bolivian
commerce. The resolution is issued under BCB authority over
the national payment system and monetary stability. Bolivia's
2014-05 prohibition is one of the earliest explicit nation-
state-level bans on bitcoin and is commonly cited alongside
the 2013-07 Thailand Bank of Thailand verbal prohibition and
the 2013-12 PBOC Notice 2013/289 as one of the first three
nation-state crypto-prohibition actions globally. The bcb.gob.bo
URL path for board resolutions is publicly indexed but specific
Wayback snapshot timestamps for the 2014-05-06 PDF have not
been pinned in this authoring pass. evidence_use=
contextual_unarchived pending re-pin in a follow-up human-audit
pass. (Resolution 044/2014 was subsequently superseded by BCB
Board Resolution No. 082/2024 of 2024-06-26, which lifted the
prohibition and authorized regulated crypto transactions via
the Bolivian banking system; that reversal is recorded in a
separate event file when authored.)

Banco Central do Brasil (BCB) Comunicado n° 25.306 dated
2014-02-19, titled "Esclarece sobre os riscos decorrentes da
aquisição das chamadas 'moedas virtuais' ou 'moedas
criptografadas' e da realização de transações com elas"
("Clarifies the risks arising from the acquisition of so-
called 'virtual currencies' or 'encrypted currencies' and
from conducting transactions with them"). The communication
distinguishes between "moedas eletrônicas" (electronic money,
regulated by Law No. 12,865 of 2013-10-09 and denominated in
Brazilian reais) and "moedas virtuais" (virtual currencies,
denominated in a unit of account distinct from sovereign-
issued currencies). The BCB warns that virtual currencies
are not issued, regulated, or guaranteed by a monetary
authority, and that some have no entity responsible for
their issuance; it notes that the volume of virtual-currency
transactions in Brazil was still low and did not pose risks
to the National Financial System. The Comunicado is a
risk-disclosure advisory addressed to the Brazil-resident
virtual-currency user class; it is not a banking-rail
severance order, an ISP/DNS block, or an enumerated-target
enforcement action. Wayback wildcard anchor is provisional;

crypto freezes can proceed without public address lists, which breaks the
standard OFAC-centric measurement methodology — there is no authoritative

settlement, or insurance services involving tokens and virtual
currencies. The pbc.gov.cn URL path format has drifted since 2017;

NEW EVENT AUTHORED — DRYRUN 2026-05-16. Phase 2 of the
2026-05-16 staged-release plan: historical-baseline P0 anchor for
the 2013-12-05 PBOC Notice 2013/289 ("Notice on Preventing Bitcoin
Risks", 关于防范比特币风险的通知, 公告 [2013]289号). Per Agent B M2
finding, this event had no candidate-ledger entry because the
non_us_state_archives source frame was planned:-not-ingested until

This event is the direct cross-temporal sibling of the already-admitted
china-pboc-crypto-ban-2021; the pair should be treated as the
canonical 2013 / 2021 PBOC comparison case in the dataset. The 2013
notice was the first comprehensive PRC central-bank action against
Bitcoin and established the regulatory frame (Bitcoin as virtual
commodity, banks excluded, exchanges treated as internet-information-
service providers under MIIT) that the 2021 nine-ministry joint
notice extended into a full ban on crypto-business activity.

Substantive findings:
- Five-ministry joint notice (PBOC + MIIT + CBRC + CSRC + CIRC).
- Bitcoin classified as a "virtual commodity," not currency.
- Financial institutions and payment service providers prohibited
  from offering Bitcoin-related services (custody / payment /
  conversion / insurance).
- Bitcoin exchanges required to register with MIIT as
  "internet information service providers" and to apply AML
  identification.
- Banks directed to refuse Bitcoin-related accounts.
- Observed cascade: within ~13 days, BTC China (~2013-12-18 CNY
  deposit pause), OKCoin, and Huobi all paused CNY deposit channels
  in compliance.

analysis_notes:
DRYRUN 2026-05-16. Phase C agent-drafted event covering the 2017-09
PBOC-led shutdown of all domestic Chinese cryptocurrency exchanges,
which ordered BTCC, OKCoin, Huobi, and smaller venues to cease
CNY-paired trading and wind down domestic operations. The triad
cluster (BTCC, OKCoin, Huobi) is the canonical subset target;
enumeration=subset reflects that the full set of affected venues
is larger than the named cluster but the triad represents the
dominant volume share. origin=agent_draft / status=draft per the

This event sits between the historical-baseline
china-pboc-crypto-ban-2013-12 (banking-rail exclusion of Bitcoin
services) and the later comparable-corpus china-pboc-crypto-ban-2021
(nine-ministry full-ban escalation), and immediately follows the
2017-09-04 ICO ban (china-ico-ban-2017-09) which was the same
regulatory cycle's first action. The 2017-09 exchange shutdown is
the load-bearing CNY-rail closure step that severed the dominant
domestic on/off-ramp surface for the entire pre-2021 PRC retail
crypto market.

Substantive findings:
- Mid-September 2017 PBOC-led administrative instruction to all
  domestic crypto exchanges to cease CNY-paired trading.
- BTCC: announced shutdown of all trading by 2017-09-30.
- Huobi, OKCoin: committed to cease yuan-paired trading by end of
  October 2017; subsequently shut down domestic CNY operations.
- Smaller venues (ViaBTC, YoBTC, Yunbi) closed in the same window.
- Offshore migration in response: Huobi → Singapore; OKCoin spinoff
  OKEx → offshore; Binance → Malta (early 2018).
- Executives of Huobi and OKCoin were temporarily barred from
  leaving Beijing during the regulatory investigation.

Why comparable_main_2017_present tier: 2017-09 sits at the leading
edge of the comparable-analysis corpus that begins 2017-01-01 per
the project's tiered analytical frame. analysis_use=comparable_analysis.

Why empirical_case rather than anchor_case: only the offramp_cex
layer carries a strong-attribution observed_change row in this
authoring pass; L4 frontend Wayback captures for the
exchange-shutdown homepage notices have not been re-verified.
Promotion to anchor_case would require the Wayback-capture pass
on L4 frontend evidence (BTCC, OKCoin, Huobi homepage notices in
late September / October 2017).

Why L0/L1/L3/asset_onchain are not_applicable: the 2017-09
instruction is a CNY-rail / licensing-rail directive, not a network
block; the Ethereum PBS-era L1/L3 measurement primitives do not
exist in 2017; Bitcoin native asset has no issuer-side admin freeze
primitive. Consistent with the 2013 and 2021 sibling treatments.

Why the primary PBOC URL is a placeholder: unlike the 2013-12 and
2021-09 PBOC notices, the 2017-09 exchange-shutdown directive was
issued administratively / verbally via the PBOC Business Management
Department (Beijing) and the Shanghai Municipal Financial Services
Office, not as a single named ministerial notice with a stable
pbc.gov.cn URL. Human audit must locate and pin the most
authoritative archival surrogate (e.g. the PBOC Business Management

reproduction) before the event may be promoted out of agent_draft.

scoped_knowledge:
The 2012-07-12 Reykjavik District Court ruling is the
pre-Bitcoin-era anchor case for court-ordered counter-
censorship at the payment-rail layer. It demonstrates that
even in the pre-blockchain financial-rail context, judicial
intervention is capable of reversing a corporate / card-
network censorship action at the merchant-services contract
layer — provided the target operator (DataCell) is
jurisdictionally co-located with a card-network sub-processor
(Valitor in Iceland) whose merchant agreement is governed by
enforceable national contract law. The Icelandic Supreme Court
subsequently affirmed the district-court order on 2013-04-24,
and a broader damages settlement was reached in 2019-07
(~7 years downstream). The case is the conceptual ancestor of
later judicial-intervention recovery dynamics that may apply
to blockchain-asset / centralized-exchange contexts: where a
national court has personal jurisdiction over a payment
intermediary and the underlying merchant agreement is
governed by enforceable national contract law, a court order
is in principle capable of restoring the payment / off-ramp
surface. The ruling has been frequently cited in the academic
and civil-society literature on financial-censorship counter-
measures (RSF, EDRi, European Parliament parliamentary
questions) as the foundational court-ordered restoration
precedent.

comparison documenting the EU Council + European Parliament's 2023-05-31
adoption of Regulation (EU) 2023/1113 — the Transfer of Funds Regulation
Recast ("TFR Recast"), the EU's zero-de-minimis Travel Rule companion
to MiCA (Regulation 2023/1114, adopted the same day). TFR Recast is the
direct supranational child of FATF Recommendation 15 (2019) and the
sibling instrument of MiCA at the EU-27 level: where MiCA establishes
the licensing / capital / custody framework for CASPs, TFR Recast layers
on the metadata-transmission obligation for every CASP-to-CASP
crypto-asset transfer regardless of amount. Effective application
2024-12-30, aligned with the MiCA CASP licensing phase.

Structural contribution to the dataset: a regulatory-framework trigger
at the metadata layer (transfer-approval gating, not asset freeze or
list publication), positioned between FATF R.15 (2019) as parent and
the national-scale Travel Rule implementations (KR FSC 2022,
India FIU offshore-VDA 2023) as siblings. Distinguishes the EU regime
by its zero-threshold posture: no de-minimis floor (vs. FATF's
recommended USD/EUR 1,000 and KR's KRW 1M ≈ USD 750), making it the
strictest known supranational Travel Rule implementation in the corpus.
Paper-relevant as the regulatory substrate for downstream EU-CASP
compliance actions expected through 2025.

coverage.note:
TFR Recast is a backend metadata-transmission obligation on CASPs; it
does not mandate frontend takedown. Individual CASPs may reconfigure
onboarding / withdrawal UI for EU users but no single-domain effect.

TFR Recast does not mandate issuer-level freeze; it constrains
transfer metadata, not the underlying asset. Asset-layer reasoning
from the OFAC USDC / USDT comparison set does not apply.

Load-bearing layer for this row: TFR Recast operationalizes via the
CASP / offramp layer by requiring originator + beneficiary KYC data
on every CASP-to-CASP crypto-asset transfer. Effective application
2024-12-30. Anchor is the EUR-Lex primary-legal artifact.

FATF "Virtual Currencies — Key Definitions and Potential AML/CFT
Risks" (2014-06-26) is the foundational supranational risk-framing
predicate for the global FATF VASP regime that culminates in the
2019-06-21 R.15 INR Travel Rule extension. The 2014 report
introduces the taxonomy ("virtual currency", "convertible / non-
convertible VC", "centralised / decentralised VC", "exchanger",
"administrator", "user", "miner") and the convertibility-as-risk-
axis frame that the subsequent FATF instruments build on. It is a
five-year regulatory development arc:
  2014-06-26  FATF VC Key Definitions report (this event)
  2015-06     FATF Guidance for a Risk-Based Approach to VCs
  2018-10     FATF Recommendations amended — VASP added to glossary
  2019-06-21  FATF R.15 INR adopting the Travel Rule for VASPs
              (fatf-r15-vasp-travel-rule-2019)
The 2014 report sits at the top of this arc as the predicate
guidance — analogous to the FinCEN FIN-2013-G001 predicate role in
the US BSA-MSB enforcement era (fincen-virtual-currency-msb-
guidance-2013) and the EBA 2014-07-04 Opinion EBA-Op-2014-08 role
in the EU regulatory development arc that culminates in the EU
MiCA Regulation 2023/1114 (eu-mica-2023).

Why null_event / null_case / observed_no_change: this event's load-
bearing function is predicate-establishing rather than cascade-
producing. The substantive regulatory effect — introducing a
shared FATF-level taxonomy and risk frame for virtual currencies —
unfolds dispersedly across the 2014→2019 regulatory development
arc rather than as a single observable point-in-time CEX
cessation directly attributable to the 2014 report alone. The
cascade-shape grammar of the schema does not natively express
class-level predicate-establishing supranational guidance, so this
event is coded honestly as null_event (0 observed_change layers) /
null_case (0 strong-attribution observed_change), with the single

citation.note:
FATF report "Virtual Currencies — Key Definitions and Potential
AML/CFT Risks," published 2014-06-26 by the Financial Action Task
Force (FATF) plenary in Paris. The report is the first FATF
instrument to engage virtual currencies (VC) substantively at
the supranational standard-setting layer. It establishes a
shared taxonomy ("virtual currency", "convertible / non-
convertible VC", "centralised / decentralised VC", "exchanger",
"administrator", "user", "miner") and a preliminary risk
assessment of money-laundering and terrorist-financing exposures
associated with virtual currency activity. The report is non-
binding guidance — it does not amend the FATF Recommendations
and does not impose Travel Rule or VASP obligations — but it
establishes the conceptual scaffolding ("exchanger" as the
regulatory locus, convertibility as the risk axis) that anchors
the subsequent five-year regulatory development arc:
(a) the 2015-06 FATF "Guidance for a Risk-Based Approach to
Virtual Currencies"; (b) the 2018-10 FATF Recommendations
amendments adding the VASP definition into the glossary;
(c) the 2019-06-21 FATF Plenary adoption of the Interpretive
Note to Recommendation 15 extending the Travel Rule to VASPs
(fatf-r15-vasp-travel-rule-2019). This 2014 report is therefore
the predicate guidance for the global FATF VASP regime.

Act's money-transmitter regulations to apply to virtual-currency
exchangers and administrators, establishing the foundational
regulatory predicate for the 2013-2016 US MSB-registration
enforcement era. observation_kind=coverage_gap with attribution=
none because the substantive cascade is dispersed across
downstream enforcement actions (Shrem/Faiella 2014, Powell 2014,
Ripple/XRP II 2015, Murgio/Coin.mx 2015) that each cite this
guidance as predicate, rather than localized to a single
observable point-in-time CEX cessation. Historical-baseline tier;
not used in main statistical denominators.

target.actor_name: Virtual currency administrators and exchangers (US BSA money transmitters)
target.enumeration_note:
Canonical target of this guidance is the regulatory class of
"administrators and exchangers" of virtual currency under the
BSA, i.e. any business that exchanges VC for fiat (or for other
VC) or that administers issuance/redemption. The class is open-
ended by construction: any US-resident person or legal entity
that comes within FinCEN's interpretation of "money transmitter"
is brought under BSA registration, AML-program, recordkeeping,
and reporting obligations prospectively. Marked enumeration=subset
rather than complete because the class is open-ended and the
membership set evolves with subsequent FinCEN administrative
rulings and enforcement actions (e.g. FIN-2014-R001 mining,
FIN-2014-R002 software development, FIN-2019-G001 CVC business-
models guidance). actor_name labels the regulated class; no
on-chain addresses or canonical_domains are enumerated because
the guidance does not designate specific entities or hosts.

citation.note:
FinCEN guidance FIN-2013-G001, "Application of FinCEN's
Regulations to Persons Administering, Exchanging, or Using
Virtual Currencies," issued 2013-03-18. The guidance interprets
FinCEN's Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) money-services-business (MSB)
regulations as applied to virtual currency (VC) and defines
three role categories: (1) users (persons who obtain VC to
purchase goods/services) — not regulated as MSBs; (2) exchangers
(persons engaged as a business in the exchange of VC for real
currency, funds, or other VC) — money transmitters and therefore
MSBs subject to BSA registration, AML program, recordkeeping,
and reporting obligations; (3) administrators (persons engaged
as a business in issuing/redeeming VC) — money transmitters and
therefore MSBs. The guidance is the foundational regulatory
predicate cited as authority in nearly every subsequent US BSA
enforcement against a virtual-currency exchanger in the
2013-2016 historical-baseline tier (Shrem/Faiella 2014, Powell
2014, Ripple/XRP II 2015, Murgio/Coin.mx 2015) and continuing
into the 2017+ comparable-analysis era (BitMEX 2020 FinCEN
concurrent action, Helix 2020 FinCEN consent assessment,
Binance 2023 FinCEN settlement). evidence_use=contextual_unarchived
because body_hash+body_path archival capture was not pinned in
this authoring pass; the live fincen.gov URL remains publicly
accessible and Wayback bracketing of the 2013 publication window
is straightforward in a follow-up human-audit pass. Provisional
year-prefix wayback anchor pending re-pin.

timestamp_sources.note:
Day-level precision per FIN-2013-G001 issuance date of
2013-03-18. The guidance carries no intra-day publication
timestamp in the public record.

comparison documenting the 2022-12-13 coordinated DOJ SDNY + SEC + CFTC
enforcement action against Samuel Bankman-Fried, FTX Trading Ltd., and
Alameda Research LLC. The federal trigger followed the 2022-11-11 FTX
Trading Ltd. voluntary Chapter 11 filing by approximately one month; the
offramp_cex withdraw-pause and customer-asset freeze were already in
effect at the trigger date via the bankruptcy estate. The retained
load-bearing observation is therefore the offramp_cex layer with
attribution=plausible rather than direct — the proximate cause of the
off-ramp shutdown is the corporate Chapter 11 instrument, and the
2022-12-13 DOJ/SEC/CFTC actions are the federal accountability layer
cascading on top.

geofencing well predates the indictment and was a 2019-era platform
bifurcation between FTX International and FTX US, not a 2022 trigger
artifact; (b) Alameda Research asset freezes are encompassed by the
Chapter 11 estate; (c) BlockFi cross-default into its own 2022-11-28
Chapter 11 filing is downstream of this row and is partially captured
by the existing blockfi-sec-lending-2022 sibling event (different
trigger — SEC 2022-02-14 lending-product settlement — but same
collapsing-platform-cluster). The bulk-Bankman-Fried criminal
disposition (2023-11-02 conviction on 7 of 8 counts, 2024-03-28
sentencing) is downstream of the 2022-12-13 trigger and is not coded
here as a separate observation.

Sibling positioning: this event sits in the S3 us-federal-enforcement
cluster alongside binance-4framework-2023 (corporate-survival cascade
with monitor), sec-v-coinbase-2023 (state-scoped staking restriction),
kraken-sec-staking-2023 (US staking-service shutdown), and

comparison shape: 2 observed_change layers (offramp_cex load-bearing,
L4 frontend secondary). Structurally a sibling of the 2021-2023
Binance EU/UK/MY/CA regulator wave (uk-fca-binance-markets-2021,
netherlands-dnb-binance-warning-2021, belgium-fsma-binance-cease-2023,
canada-csa-binance-withdrawal-2023) but distinct in two respects.
First, the German action is a licence-application withdrawal by the
operator following a supervisory signal that approval would not be
forthcoming — there is no published BaFin denial or cease-and-desist
press item. Second, the operational effect is a full EU-market
pre-MiCA exit at the Germany cohort: BaFin's KWG crypto-custody
licensing regime (sec. 1 para. 1a sentence 2 no. 6) is the
pre-MiCA German-national framework, and the licence-application
withdrawal closes the path to a regulated-in-DE Binance offering
before the MiCA EEA-passporting framework comes into force.

Paper-relevant contrast vs UK FCA (uk-fca-binance-markets-2021):
FCA-2021 produced a class-wide GBP payment-rail severance through
retail-bank responses to the consumer warning; BaFin-2023 produced

Vector / A7 Russian virtual-currency network, framed by Treasury as the operational
successor to Garantex (originally designated 2022-04-05; see garantex-ofac-2022).

censoring-relay share from 0% to 86% three days after the event (2025-08-17), settling to

responses were either null (single-wallet designations) or gradual post-PBS ramps

relay-ecosystem composition change (a single large-share relay flipping policy) rather than
a direct Grinex-address-driven filter update; pending per-relay data, attribution is
marked unknown.

relays drove it and whether their block-filter lists added the Grinex 8 ETH addresses;

probability of fresh freezes given Tether's typical response time); (3) pinned

comparison documenting the Hong Kong Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656)
commencement on 2025-08-01 — the first HKMA-administered stablecoin
issuer licensing regime globally for fiat-referenced stablecoins (FRS).
Unlike sanction-style enforcement (S1/S2 OFAC), this is a regulatory-
framework trigger: criminal-penalty-backed licensing of stablecoin
issuance as a regulated activity (HK$5M fine + 7yr imprisonment for
unlicensed conduct). Structurally closest to EU MiCA (eu-mica-2023) as
a supranational/national regulatory framework establishing licensing
preconditions for stablecoin issuance, and to the HK SFC VATP licensing
regime (hongkong-sfc-vatp-licensing-2023-06) as a parallel HK-side

NEW EVENT AUTHORED — agent_draft 2026-05-16. Historical-baseline
contextual case for the 2014-03-19 Central Bank of Iceland
(Seðlabanki Íslands / CBI) statement "Significant risk attached
to use of virtual currency", which articulated the CBI's
interpretation that purchases of bitcoin by Icelandic residents
are prohibited under the Iceland Foreign Exchange Act (Act
No. 87/1992, as amended) and the post-2008-banking-crisis
capital-controls regime. Authored at status=draft pending human
audit of (i) the cb.is and sedlabanki.is URL reachability and
Wayback snapshot pinning, (ii) the LoC Global Legal Monitor
English-language summary anchor, and (iii) any exchange-side
evidence of Iceland-resident-cutoff that may exist in
contemporaneous press coverage but was not located in this
authoring pass.

Significance: this is the first nation-state action explicitly
treating bitcoin purchases as prohibited under existing FX-control
law rather than under a freshly issued crypto-specific directive.
It is the contextual sibling of china-pboc-crypto-ban-2013-12
(PBOC Notice 2013/289 of 2013-12-05) — the China 2013 notice
acted via banking-and-payments-rail prohibitions, while the
Iceland 2014 statement acts via capital-controls FX-law
reinterpretation. Together they form the earliest pair of
nation-state-level bitcoin-restriction events in the dataset.

Why historical_baseline_2013_2016 tier: 2014 belongs to the
pre-2017 historical-baseline tier per sampling/frame.yaml.
analysis_use=contextual_baseline excludes this row from the
2017+ comparable-analysis denominator. The event is retained as
contextual case-study material rather than as a denominator row
because (a) it predates the comparable corpus and (b) the
cascade surface is class-level rather than exchange-specific.

Why empirical_case rather than anchor_case: the offramp_cex
observation is observation_kind=not_observed with
attribution=plausible, not an observed_change row. The CBI
statement clearly carries direct-attribution force on
Icelandic-resident bitcoin-buying behaviour as a class, but
the cascade surface in the available public record is not
exchange-specific. Without a documented exchange-side cutoff
or a measured Iceland-resident on-chain volume shift, the
event admits only at empirical_case strength.

Why L0/L1/L3/L4/asset_onchain are not_applicable: the CBI
statement is a legal-interpretation notice under existing
FX-control law; it does not direct network-layer blocking,
L4 frontend changes, or engage any 2014-nonexistent L1/L3 PBS
measurement primitive or any asset-issuer admin path. The
L0/L1/L3/asset_onchain not_applicable treatment matches the
sibling 2013 PBOC / 2018 RBI / 2021 PBOC banking-rail-severance
pattern.

Post-2014 trajectory: Iceland's broader capital-controls regime
was substantially liberalised in 2017 (CBI New Rules on Foreign
Exchange, 2017-03-12), which effectively lifted the indirect
bitcoin-purchase prohibition. That 2017 amendment is a natural
candidate for a separate recovery / sibling-event row but is
not authored in this pass.

coverage.note:
The 2014-03-19 CBI statement does not direct ISP-level domain
blocking, DNS interference, or network-layer action; it is a
legal-interpretation notice under existing FX-control law.

Coverage scope: Iceland-resident off-ramp cutoffs documented

The CBI statement is by construction an off-ramp-layer signal:
it tells Icelandic residents that purchasing bitcoin from
foreign exchanges violates the Foreign Exchange Act. The

public record (English and Icelandic press, exchange status
pages, LoC Global Legal Monitor) for the 90 days following
the 2014-03-19 release: no specific exchange is documented

and the dominant 2014 bitcoin exchanges (Bitstamp, Bitfinex,
Mt. Gox in its pre-collapse and collapse phases) did not

real but not exchange-side observable in this authoring pass.

regime, but it does not name any specific exchange as having

scoped_claim:
The Central Bank of Iceland (Seðlabanki Íslands) news release of
2014-03-19, "Significant risk attached to use of virtual currency",
stated the CBI's interpretation that purchases of bitcoin by
Icelandic residents are prohibited under the Iceland Foreign
Exchange Act and the post-2008 capital-controls regime. The
cascade surface is class-level on Icelandic residents; no
exchange-side Iceland-resident cutoff is documented in this
authoring pass, so offramp_cex carries an observation_kind=not_observed
row with attribution=plausible.
scoped_knowledge:
This event is the earliest dataset case of a nation-state acting
against bitcoin via reinterpretation of pre-existing capital-
controls / FX-control law, rather than via a freshly issued
crypto-specific directive. The contrast with china-pboc-crypto-ban-
2013-12 (which acted via a five-ministry crypto-specific notice
prohibiting bank services to bitcoin) is informative: both events
produce a banking-rail-severance shape, but the Iceland 2014
legal mechanism is FX-law-reuse rather than crypto-specific
rule-making. The cascade surface is class-level rather than
exchange-specific because Iceland's bitcoin market in 2014 was
small relative to the PRC market and because the CBI statement
did not name specific exchanges. The 2017 CBI New Rules on
Foreign Exchange materially relaxed the capital-controls regime,
effectively rendering the 2014 interpretation moot — that
recovery dynamic is a candidate sibling event for future
authoring.

target.enumeration_note:
Target is the class of Icelandic residents engaged in or
contemplating bitcoin purchases (and by extension other virtual-
currency purchases). The CBI statement does not enumerate

states a legal interpretation that applies to the entire class

Exchange Act. No specific exchange is named as the target,
so canonical_domains is empty.

citation.note:
Central Bank of Iceland (Seðlabanki Íslands / CBI) news release
dated 2014-03-19 titled "Significant risk attached to use of
virtual currency". The statement, issued in the days leading up
to the Auroracoin (AUR) airdrop launch, examines the legal
status of virtual currencies (bitcoin, Auroracoin) under
Icelandic law and the Iceland Foreign Exchange Act (Act
No. 87/1992 on Foreign Exchange, as amended after the 2008
banking-crisis capital-controls regime). Core position
articulated by the CBI: (1) bitcoin and Auroracoin are not
recognised currency or legal tender in the sense of Icelandic
law; (2) it is prohibited to engage in foreign-exchange trading
with the electronic currency bitcoin under the Foreign Exchange
Act, because Icelandic-resident purchases of bitcoin from
foreign counterparties constitute movement of capital out of
Iceland which is restricted under the post-2008 capital
controls; (3) Icelandic residents should be cautious about
using virtual currencies given the absence of consumer
protection and the foreign-exchange-law exposure. The CBI is
the only authority with rule-making power under the FX Act,
so this statement carries the legal interpretation that
bitcoin purchases by Icelandic residents are restricted by
existing FX-control law. The cb.is URL path is the canonical
publication anchor; specific Wayback snapshot timestamp
requires re-pinning in human audit before this citation may
serve as an admission anchor.

Icelandic-language mirror of the same 2014-03-19 CBI news
release on the sedlabanki.is domain. Carries identical
substantive content to the cb.is English statement. Marked
evidence_use=contextual_unarchived; specific Wayback snapshot
timestamp requires re-pinning in human audit.

US Library of Congress Global Legal Monitor entry titled
"Iceland: National Digital Currency Auroracoin Launched"
dated 2014-08-12, providing an English-language summary
of the CBI 2014-03-19 position and characterising it as an
interpretation of the Foreign Exchange Act restricting
Icelandic-resident purchases of bitcoin (since such
purchases entail capital movement out of Iceland that the
post-2008 capital-controls regime prohibits). Used here as
a contextual translation anchor. Specific Wayback snapshot
timestamp requires re-pinning in human audit.

driven by a US comprehensive-sanctions Executive Order.** Within
10 days of the 2022-02-21 EO 14065 (comprehensive sanctions on

corporate-policy character is what makes this a paper-relevant

corporate-policy-driven, not OFAC-compelled" claim, and

null_event documenting the 2023-06-01 commencement of the Japan
Payment Services Act Amendment Act establishing the Electronic
Payment Instrument (EPI / 電子決済手段) regulatory regime for
fiat-referenced stablecoins. First major industrial-democracy
stablecoin issuer regime globally — predating EU MiCA's stablecoin
provisions (effective 2024-06-30) and the HK HKMA Stablecoins
Ordinance (effective 2025-08-01). Structurally distinct from the
EU and HK regimes in three ways: (1) JP restricts EPI issuance to a
closed list of three pre-existing licensed entity classes (banks,
fund transfer service providers, trust companies/banks) rather than
creating a new stablecoin-issuer licence category; (2) JP separates
issuer regulation from intermediary regulation via the parallel
EPIESP registration regime; (3) JP's foreign-stablecoin treatment
permits intermediation by domestic EPIESPs subject to JP-side
reserve backing equal to intermediated balances, rather than the
EU MiCA equivalence-passport model or the HK extraterritorial
HKD-peg coverage.

Coded null_event / null_case because (a) no JP-issued EPI was
launched at the 2023-06-01 commencement date, (b) pre-existing
JP-registered-VASP behavior (no USDT/USDC listings as of 2022-11)
produces no observable post-commencement delisting cascade, and

Binance Japan 2025) are forward-looking cascade events that will

regulatory-framework trigger; downstream EPIESP-registration and

Paper-relevant contrast vs eu-mica-2023: both 2023-06 stablecoin
regulatory-framework triggers, but JP commences on 2023-06-01 with
the issuer/intermediary regime live whereas EU MiCA OJ-publishes on
2023-06-09 with stablecoin provisions deferred to 2024-06-30 and
full CASP licensing to 2024-12-30. JP is therefore the first
industrial-democracy stablecoin issuer regime to take legal effect.

Paper-relevant contrast vs hongkong-hkma-stablecoins-ordinance-2025:
HK creates a new HKMA-administered stablecoin-issuer licence
category with criminal penalties (HK$5M + 7yr) for unlicensed
conduct and extraterritorial application to HKD-pegged stablecoins
globally; JP uses a closed list of three pre-existing licensed
entity classes with administrative (not criminal) supervisory
enforcement and territorial application limited to JP-resident-
facing intermediation. JP is the earlier and structurally lighter
regime; HK is the later and structurally heavier regime.

comparison documenting the OECD's 2022-10-10 Crypto-Asset Reporting
Framework (CARF) publication — the first binding supranational
crypto tax-reporting standard. CARF is a companion to the 2014
Common Reporting Standard (CRS) and operates at the OECD level with
G20 endorsement, distinct from EU-level instruments like MiCA
(eu-mica-2023) and FATF-level instruments like Recommendation 15 +
the VASP Travel Rule (fatf-r15-vasp-travel-rule-2019). Together
these three supranational instruments form the regulatory substrate
layer of the dataset: CARF (tax-reporting), MiCA (market-conduct +
licensing), FATF R.15 (AML / Travel Rule). Each operates on the
RCASP / CASP / VASP entity class with overlapping but distinct
reporting and conduct obligations.

Load-bearing structure: offramp_cex is the load-bearing observation
axis. CARF defines the RCASP entity class and mandates transaction-
level reporting to domestic tax authorities (then automatically
exchanged across jurisdictions under CRS-equivalent mechanics). The
framework is metadata-collection at the off-ramp interface — distinct

target.enumeration_note:
Reporting Crypto-Asset Service Providers (RCASPs) operating in CARF-
adopting jurisdictions. RCASPs are defined to include centralized
crypto exchanges (Coinbase, Kraken, Binance country entities,
Bitstamp, Bitpanda, etc.), brokers, dealers, and operators of crypto
ATMs that effectuate relevant exchange transactions in crypto-assets
as a business. Self-hosted (non-custodial) wallets and most peer-to-
peer protocol activity remain out of scope at the protocol level,
but RCASP-intermediated transfers to / from self-custody addresses
fall within the reporting perimeter when the RCASP is the
counterparty. No address-level enumeration — this is sector-wide
tax-reporting regulation operating at the RCASP entity class.

citation.note:
OECD Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF) published 2022-10-10 by
the OECD Committee on Fiscal Affairs at the request of the G20. CARF
is the first binding supranational crypto tax-reporting standard,
functioning as a companion to the Common Reporting Standard (CRS)
first published 2014. The instrument mandates that Reporting
Crypto-Asset Service Providers (RCASPs) — broadly defined to cover
centralized exchanges, brokers, dealers, and operators of crypto
ATMs — collect and transmit transaction-level reporting on relevant
crypto-asset transactions to their domestic tax authorities, which
then automatically exchange the data with partner jurisdictions
under the CRS multilateral framework. Companion amendments to CRS
were issued in the same publication to capture central-bank digital
currencies and specified electronic money products. The 2022-10-10
publication is the foundational instrument; subsequent OECD work
delivered the Multilateral Competent Authority Agreement (MCAA) for
CARF on 2023-11-10, with the first reporting under CARF scheduled
for 2027 (covering 2026 calendar-year transactions) in 48+
jurisdictions that committed to early adoption in the 2023-11-10
joint statement.

Day-level via the 2022-10-10 OECD publication date. CARF was

released for public consultation between March-May 2022; the
2022-10-10 release is the finalized binding text.

citation.note:
FinCEN press release dated 2015-05-05: "FinCEN Fines Ripple Labs
Inc. in First Civil Enforcement Action Against a Virtual Currency
Exchanger." Announced jointly with the US Attorney's Office for
the Northern District of California. Core terms: (1) $700,000
civil monetary penalty assessed by FinCEN against Ripple Labs
Inc. and its wholly-owned subsidiary XRP II, LLC for willful
violations of the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA), including (a) acting
as a money services business (MSB) without registering with
FinCEN, and (b) failing to implement and maintain an adequate
anti-money-laundering (AML) program in connection with the sale
of XRP virtual currency; (2) settlement agreement requiring
Ripple Labs and XRP II to undertake remedial measures including
appointment of an independent reviewer, enhanced AML program,
SAR retroactive review, and structural compliance changes; (3)
a separate non-prosecution agreement (NPA) with the US Attorney's
Office N.D. Cal. resolving the criminal investigation, conditioned
on the FinCEN settlement and on Ripple's adoption of the
compliance undertakings. This is the FIRST civil enforcement
action by FinCEN against a virtual-currency exchanger and a
canonical historical-baseline anchor for the
FinCEN-as-virtual-currency-regulator posture established under
the 2013-03-18 FinCEN guidance (FIN-2013-G001).

centralized-exchange delistings of XRP, with each exchange's official
announcement explicitly citing the SEC filing as the legal cause. The

exchange-scoped service restriction rather than third-party listing
removal): here the SEC named the token issuer, and the cascade is

Structural significance: SEC v. Telegram Group Inc. (No. 19-cv-9439,
SDNY, Judge P. Kevin Castel) is the landmark SAFT-framework
decision in U.S. crypto-securities enforcement. Telegram argued the
Simple Agreement for Future Tokens sale to accredited investors and
the later token delivery were legally distinct transactions — the
SAFT-being-a-security-but-the-token-not architecture promoted by
practitioners following the 2017 ICO wave. Judge Castel rejected
that severance under a Gary Plastic resale-analysis reading of
Howey: the initial purchasers were treated as statutory underwriters
whose contemplated resales into a public market collapsed the
primary and secondary transactions into a single unregistered
public offering of securities. This precedent reshaped the SAFT
fundraising template and is regularly cited in subsequent SEC
unregistered-token cases (and forms part of the legal background
for related-event rows including sec-v-coinbase-2023 and
blockfi-sec-lending-2022).

The measurable observation is intentionally narrow: an issuer-level
cancellation of a planned token distribution + the foreclosed
public-CEX listing cascade. Gram never launched on public CEXs,
not because exchanges delisted it, but because the issuer-side
distribution itself was injunction-triggered cancelled. This is
why offramp_cex is the load-bearing layer rather than a stub L4
takedown or a token-delisting claim. The dataset does not assert
ISP-level blocking of telegram.org / ton.org, a frontend takedown,
on-chain admin-method engagement (Gram had no live such primitive),
or specific secondary-market delisting actions by named CEXs (none
occurred because there was no token to list).

Pairs with cftc-v-ooki-dao-2022 (legal-personhood / DAO-as-target
enforcement at the modern endpoint of U.S. crypto-civil-action
reach) and sec-v-coinbase-2023 (entity-level unregistered-
securities theory against an operating exchange). All three are
S3 securities/derivatives civil actions where the load-bearing
observation is an operator-state or issuer-state change rather
than a chain-level filter.

citation.note:
SEC press release 2020-69 (2020-03-24): "Court Orders Preliminary
Injunction in Telegram Case." SDNY (Judge P. Kevin Castel) granted
the SEC's motion for a preliminary injunction halting Telegram
Group Inc. and TON Issuer Inc. from distributing the approximately
2.9 billion Gram digital tokens to the 175 initial purchasers
(and ultimately to the secondary market) from the October 2017 -
March 2018 private placement that raised roughly $1.7 billion.
The court applied the Howey test plus the Gary Plastic resale-
analysis doctrine and concluded the Gram distribution constituted
an unregistered offering of securities under Section 5 of the
Securities Act of 1933, because the initial purchasers stood as
statutory underwriters reselling into a public market. This is the
landmark SAFT-framework ("Simple Agreement for Future Tokens")
decision: the court rejected Telegram's argument that the SAFT
sale to accredited investors and the later token delivery were
legally distinct transactions, holding instead that they were
steps in a single unregistered public offering. Marked

FINMA's 2018-02-16 "Guidelines for enquiries regarding the
regulatory framework for initial coin offerings (ICOs)" (the
FINMA ICO-Wegleitung) is the foundational Swiss-jurisdiction
framework instrument categorizing tokens into three classes
for the purpose of assessing ICO regulatory treatment:
  - Payment tokens (cryptocurrencies; GwG/AML obligations once
    tradeable)
  - Utility tokens (digital access rights; outside securities
    scope only if sole-purpose and usable at issuance)
  - Asset tokens (participations / dividends / interest claims;
    treated as securities under Swiss Code of Obligations
    prospectus rules)
Hybrid forms are explicitly contemplated. The framework is the
Swiss-jurisdiction analogue to the EU MiCA tripartite token
taxonomy (e-money tokens / asset-referenced tokens / other
crypto-assets) that arrives five years later in MiCA
2023/1114 (eu-mica-2023), and it sits in the same family of
2018-era national/supranational framework-guidance instruments
that crystallized the post-2017-ICO-bubble regulatory frame
(cf. Japan FSA's 2018-01-29 Coincheck order
japan-fsa-coincheck-orders-2018, which is reactive single-
entity supervision rather than framework taxonomy).

Tezos Foundation (Zug, CH) is the load-bearing illustrative
target: its 2017-07 ICO (~USD 232M raised on ~30,000 BTC + ~
366,000 ETH contributed) was the largest 2017-cohort Swiss
ICO and sat in the Swiss Zug-foundation issuance pattern the
guidelines clarify. The concurrent Tezos governance dispute
(Foundation president Johann Gevers vs co-founders
Arthur & Kathleen Breitman / Dynamic Ledger Solutions) over
the disposition of contributed funds escalated through 2017-
10 to 2018-02 and was the highest-profile Swiss-ICO
governance crisis at the time the guidelines were drafted.
However, the guidelines themselves are framework guidance,
not a per-entity enforcement order — they do not name Tezos,
do not designate Tezos addresses, and do not impose a
bilateral remediation regime on the Tezos Foundation. The
retroactive impact is the application of the tripartite
classification framework to the 2017-cohort token issuances,
which subsequent FINMA enquiry responses to individual
sponsors (the no-action enquiry process) operationalize on a
case-by-case basis. Other 2017-cohort Swiss ICOs in scope
include Cardano Foundation (Zug), DFINITY (Zurich), Bancor /
BProtocol Foundation (Zug), and Status (formerly Zug).

Why null_event / null_case / observed_no_change: this event's
load-bearing function is framework predicate-establishing
rather than cascade-producing. The substantive regulatory
effect — introducing the Swiss-jurisdiction tripartite
payment / utility / asset token taxonomy and the corresponding
Swiss-financial-market-law treatment matrix — unfolds
dispersedly across the per-sponsor FINMA enquiry process
rather than as a single observable point-in-time cascade
directly attributable to the 2018-02-16 release alone. The
cascade-shape grammar of the schema does not natively express
framework-level token-classification guidance, so this event
is coded honestly as null_event (0 observed_change layers) /
null_case (0 strong-attribution observed_change), with the
single observation row expressing the framework predicate as
observed_no_change with attribution=none at the
token-classification axis per the schema constraint that
observed_no_change rows take attribution=none.

Why comparable_main_2017_present tier: 2018-02 belongs to the
comparable_main_2017_present temporal tier per the 2008+
tiered frame. analysis_use=comparable_analysis matches the
validator's tier-vs-analysis-use consistency rule
(validate.py); the row will sit in the comparable denominator
as a null_case framework-predicate row, analogous to the EU
MiCA framework precedent (eu-mica-2023) at the supranational
level.

citation.note:
Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA /
Eidgenössische Finanzmarktaufsicht) press release and accompanying
"Guidelines for enquiries regarding the regulatory framework for
initial coin offerings (ICOs)" (FINMA ICO-Wegleitung) published
2018-02-16. The guidelines establish FINMA's tripartite token
taxonomy for the purpose of assessing ICO regulatory treatment
under Swiss financial market law:
  (1) Payment tokens (Zahlungs-Token) — synonymous with
      cryptocurrencies, no further functions or links to
      development projects; treated as means of payment and
      subject to Swiss Anti-Money Laundering Act (GwG) obligations
      once tradeable / transferable.
  (2) Utility tokens (Nutzungs-Token) — confer digital access
      rights to an application or service; not treated as
      securities under Swiss law if their sole purpose is access
      and they are usable at issuance.
  (3) Asset tokens (Anlage-Token) — represent assets such as
      participations in real underlyings, companies, earnings
      streams, or entitlements to dividends/interest; treated as
      securities, with attendant prospectus / civil-law
      requirements under the Swiss Code of Obligations.
The framework explicitly contemplates hybrid forms (e.g. utility
tokens with payment-token characteristics simultaneously falling
under GwG). The guidelines apply retroactively as the framework
FINMA uses when ICO sponsors request a no-action enquiry; this
affects Zug-based ICO sponsors from the 2017 cohort, including
Tezos Foundation (Zug), whose 2017-07 ICO raised ~USD 232M and
whose post-ICO governance dispute between the Foundation
(Johann Gevers) and the Breitman family (Dynamic Ledger
Solutions) escalated concurrent with FINMA's broader Swiss-ICO
scrutiny. The guidelines themselves are framework guidance, not
a per-entity enforcement order — they do not name Tezos or any
other 2017-cohort issuer. evidence_use=contextual_unarchived
because body_hash + body_path archival capture was not pinned in
this agent-authoring pass; Wayback anchor is a year-prefix
bracket pending re-pin by the human auditor.

**NEW EVENT AUTHORED — DRYRUN 2026-05-17**. Phase E pre-Bitcoin-baseline
follow-on / Phase B historical-baseline 2013-2016 admit-pass: foundational
pre-2017 non-US central-bank action against Bitcoin. Authored by LLM agent
in this pass at origin=agent_draft and status=draft per the task brief;
human review required to (i) re-pin Wayback snapshots for the CoinDesk and
Bangkok Post anchors, (ii) verify the corporate-source Bitcoin Co. Ltd
suspension-notice text against the v0.3 Wayback body_hash/body_path
primary_corporate anchor, and (iii) decide whether to upgrade to
origin=human_reviewed.

Substantive findings:
- 2013-07-29 Bank of Thailand (BOT) Foreign Exchange Administration and
  Policy Department held a meeting with Bitcoin Co. Ltd (a Thailand-
  incorporated bitcoin exchange that had voluntarily approached the BOT
  seeking clearance to operate).
- BOT verbally advised that, due to (a) lack of existing applicable
  Thai laws covering bitcoin, (b) capital controls under the Exchange
  Control Act B.E. 2485 (1942) which gives the BOT competent-officer
  authority over foreign-exchange transactions, and (c) the multi-facet
  nature of bitcoin straddling currency, commodity, and payment
  functions, the following bitcoin activities were illegal in
  Thailand: purchase or sale of bitcoins; purchase or sale of goods or
  services for bitcoins; sending or receiving bitcoins across the
  Thai border.
- BOT did not publish a written regulation; the advisement was
  verbal. Bitcoin Co. Ltd posted a public statement on its website
  the same day announcing suspension of operations.
- The suspension lasted approximately 6.5 months until 2014-02-15,
  when Bitcoin Co. Ltd resumed services following a BOT clarification
  letter (dated 2014-01-31) stating that bitcoin trading fell outside
  the BOT's regulatory scope. BOT subsequently introduced ambiguity
  by suggesting the operator had over-interpreted the clarification.

Why trigger.type=regulatory_enforcement: per codebook §5.1, the BOT
advisement is a non-US national-regulator administrative action
(specifically an informal verbal directive under the Exchange Control
Act framework), not a network-layer or ISP-level block. This matches
the 2026-05-17 codebook addition formalizing regulatory_enforcement
as the canonical trigger type for non-US national-regulator
administrative enforcement actions distinct from nation_state_block
(which is reserved for ISP/DNS/payment-rail blocks).

Why temporal_tier=historical_baseline_2013_2016 and
analysis_use=historical_baseline: per codebook §6 and the project's
2008+ tiered frame, events in the 2013-2016 window belong to the
historical-baseline tier and excluded from the 2017+ comparable-
analysis denominator. Canonical form per §6 — alias
"contextual_baseline" is NOT accepted by the validator.

Why empirical_shape=comparison: per codebook §3, only the offramp_cex
layer carries an observed_change row in this event (one
observed_change → comparison, not cascade). L0/L1/L3/asset_onchain
are not_applicable on construct-did-not-exist or scope-mismatch
grounds; L4 frontend is not_measured pending Wayback capture of the
Bitcoin Co. Ltd 2013-07 suspension-notice page.

Why admission_tier=empirical_case: per codebook §4, exactly one
strong-attribution (direct) observed_change row exists at
offramp_cex; this admits the event at empirical_case, below the
≥ 2 strong-attribution rows that would be required for anchor_case.

Why attribution=direct on the offramp_cex observation: under
codebook §1.2-§1.5 logic adapted to a non-US regulatory enforcement
trigger: (i) the BOT advisement directly named Bitcoin Co. Ltd's
proposed bitcoin-exchange business as the subject of the meeting

Foundational comparison-shape S5 corporate-policy-change event:
this is the earliest documented L4 DeFi-frontend voluntary self-
censorship action in the corpus, predating the 2022-08-08 OFAC SDN
designation of Tornado Cash (tornado-cash-ofac-2022) by 116 days
(~4 months). Paper-relevant precisely because it isolates the
protocol-team-initiated frontend filtering archetype before any
government compulsion existed. The Tornado Cash team — the same
team that would later be criminally targeted (see
tornado-cash-storm-conviction-2025) — chose voluntarily to deploy
the Chainalysis on-chain sanctions-screening oracle contract at
the tornado.cash dapp, blocking OFAC SDN addresses from the
user-facing frontend while leaving the underlying smart contracts
permissionless. This is the seed instance of the "frontend /
protocol-layer split" archetype later instantiated by the
2022-08 cascade: aave-tornado-frontend-block-2022-08,
uniswap-balancer-tornado-frontend-block-2022-08,
infura-alchemy-tornado-rpc-block-2022, and
circle-usdc-tornado-2022. The 2022-04-15 timing follows the
2022-04-14 OFAC redesignation of the DPRK Lazarus Group with the
Ronin Bridge hack address universe — Tornado Cash's voluntary
action is causally consistent with that upstream OFAC pressure on
the broader address space, but Tornado Cash itself was not named
in any OFAC action until 2022-08-08.

analysis_notes:
Reverse-cascade pilot with direct operator attribution on two of six
layers. The trigger is the 2025-03-21 OFAC delisting. At the asset layer,
a concrete on-chain USDC unblacklist transaction for one target address
lands on 2025-03-22 (primary_onchain, direct). At the frontend layer, the
2025-03-25 operator commit 2437ecc426 on the maintained classic-ui Gitea
repo explicitly undoes the sanctions-era frontend freeze: the block
comment "Instances frozen due to sanctions" is removed from
networkConfig.js, restoring USDC pool configuration, and the sanctions-era
backup domain 2.torndao.eth.limo is swapped out for tornadocash.eth.limo
across the UI head, gateway whitelist, and six localized compliance
warnings. The removed comment is a first-party operator acknowledgement
that the prior code state was a sanctions response; this upgrades L4
attribution from plausible to direct. Official Tornado Cash docs
current-state capture bundle confirms that the UI remains reachable. L0 and
off-ramp rollback remain in coverage rather than observations. The event
stays a cascade by layer count (three changed layers), while only some layers
have direct attribution.

analysis_notes:
comparison documenting the 2022-11-08 OFAC redesignation of Tornado Cash under
DPRK-related authorities (simultaneously removing the original 2022-08-08 Cyber-related
designation). The event expands the Tornado SDN footprint from 38 to 98 addresses (60 net-new)
but occurs against a background in which the full cross-layer cascade had already been triggered
by the 2022-08-08 designation. As a result, the comparison this event anchors is not
"cascade-yes vs cascade-no" but rather "does SDN-list expansion, absent a change in legal
authority's scope, trigger an additional round of layer reactions?"

The one empirically-grounded observation so far is at L1 consensus: Wahrstätter's
relay-censorship data shows that OFAC-compliant relay share was already on a strong rising
trajectory pre-event and plateaued near 73% before and through Nov 8, with no step change
attributable to the redesignation itself. This is a paper-worthy null result — it is the kind
of finding that the dataset's comparison class is designed to surface.

Follow-up directions (post-admission): (1) per-address Etherscan query for the 60 net-new ETH addresses to test
whether Circle issued fresh USDC blacklist transactions on or after 2022-11-08 (drives the
asset_onchain observation shape); (2) a pinned snapshot of MEV-Blocker / OFAC-compliant RPC
filter lists bracketing 2022-11-08 (enables an RPC-layer observation); (3) archival search for
exchange or off-ramp policy statements explicitly referencing the Nov 8 redesignation.

Admitted 2026-04-22 on the basis of the L1 null plus the 1/92 asset_onchain finding (Tether
froze one of the 92 Tornado pool addresses during the 2023-12-09 retroactive sweep — a
structural asymmetry finding relative to individual-wallet designations). RPC / off-ramp
layers remain scoped for follow-up.

is the conviction milestone of the criminal-prosecution chain that
began with the 2023-08-23 indictment (admitted as null_case because
the indictment alone produced no measured cross-layer cascade). The
verdict event is admitted SEPARATELY because the conviction (not the
indictment) is the first US developer-liability precedent on the
§ 1960 unlicensed-MTB theory against a non-custodial privacy protocol
— a load-bearing legal-doctrinal milestone distinct from the
charging-document stage. Care: do NOT double-count developer-
enforcement cascade artifacts at both events; the 2023-08-23 indictment
event holds the indictment+OFAC-companion null-cascade evidence, while
this 2025-08-06 verdict event holds the conviction-precedent + operator-
narrative chilling-effect layer.

Load-bearing structure: asset_onchain layer is the load-bearing axis,
carrying TWO conceptual phenomena: (1) observed_no_change at
attribution=none on the Tornado Cash contract substrate — the 98 mixer
contracts continued live post-verdict because the conviction targets
the developer (Storm), not the immutable non-custodial protocol code;
(2) the **operator-narrative** observed_change at attribution=plausible
is recorded on L4 frontend rather than asset_onchain (the validator
requires primary_onchain sources for asset_onchain observed_change
rows; the operator-narrative chilling-effect channel does not have a
tx_hash-backed substrate, so it is recorded on the L4 ecosystem axis
where developer-repository state lives). This structural decomposition
is the paper-worthy contribution: the first US developer-criminal-
conviction for protocol-authoring produced zero on-chain cascade
(contracts immutable, non-custodial) but a non-zero ecosystem-level
personal-risk-reassessment channel for similar privacy-tool authors.

cascade anchor) and tornado-cash-ofac-delisting-2025 (2025-03-21 OFAC
removal, reverse-cascade anchor): the verdict sits ~4.5 months AFTER
the OFAC delisting — a temporally awkward ordering where the protocol

litigation pressure while DOJ pressed forward with the criminal

null_event documenting Turkey's 2024-07-02 enactment of Law No.
7518 amending the Capital Markets Law (CMK / Law 6362) to
establish a comprehensive CASP licensing regime under the Capital
Markets Board (CMB / Sermaye Piyasası Kurulu / SPK). The law
grants the CMB authority to license, supervise, and sanction
Crypto Asset Service Providers operating in Turkey, introduces a
customer-asset segregation obligation, and sets a transition
window for incumbent operators (BtcTurk, Paribu, ICRYPEX,
Bitexen, Binance TR, etc.) to file license applications.
Secondary regulations (Communiqués III-35/B.1 platform services
and III-35/B.2 custody-only) published 2025-03-13 specify TRY
100M minimum charter capital for platforms and TRY 50M for
custody-only entities.

Follow-on to turkey-cbrt-crypto-ban-2021: the 2021 CBRT
regulation severed the payment-rail on-ramp (banning crypto in
payments) but left exchanges formally operational; Law 7518

HMRC Revenue & Customs Brief 09/14 ("Bitcoin and other
cryptocurrencies") published 2014-03-03 by HM Revenue &
Customs setting out HMRC's position on the tax treatment
of income from and charges in connection with activities
involving bitcoin and other similar cryptocurrencies,
specifically for VAT, Corporation Tax, Income Tax, and
Capital Gains Tax. Key VAT positions: (i) income from
bitcoin mining is generally outside the scope of VAT
because mining is not an economic activity for VAT
purposes (insufficient link between services provided and
consideration received); (ii) when bitcoin is exchanged
for sterling or foreign currencies, no VAT is due on the
value of the bitcoins themselves, and exchange-side fees
for arranging or carrying out such transactions are also
VAT-exempt; (iii) VAT applies in the normal way to
suppliers of goods or services sold in exchange for
bitcoin, with the supply valued in sterling at the
transaction point. HMRC framed the VAT guidance as
provisional pending further EU regulatory development;
the position was subsequently aligned with the CJEU's
2015-10-22 Hedqvist judgment (C-264/14) treating bitcoin
exchange as a VAT-exempt financial-services transaction.

Tax Journal 2014-03-06 contemporaneous summary "HMRC
issues guidance on bitcoin", corroborating the 2014-03-03
publication date and the VAT-exemption framing for

comparison documenting Ukraine's 2022-03-16 enactment of the Law "On
Virtual Assets" (Bill 3637) signed by President Volodymyr Zelensky two
and a half weeks after the start of the Russian invasion (2022-02-24).
The law establishes the legal status, classification, and ownership
rules for virtual assets in Ukraine and designates the National
Securities and Stock Market Commission (NSSMC) as primary regulator
of the virtual asset market, with the National Bank of Ukraine
retaining authority over asset-backed virtual assets. The law mandates
registration / licensing of Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs)
operating in or servicing Ukrainian users.

**Honest dual-character note.** The Law "On Virtual Assets" is
permissive in framing — it legalizes the asset class in Ukraine,
enables UA-domiciled crypto businesses to open domestic bank
accounts, and provides the legal substrate for the wartime
crypto-donation surge that brought ~USD 100M of crypto donations
into Ukrainian government and military wallets by mid-2022. At the
same time it is compliance-mandating at the offramp_cex layer: any
VASP servicing UA users becomes subject to NSSMC licensing,
effectively bringing offshore exchanges into a UA compliance regime
for their UA-user relationships. trigger.type=nation_state_block is
the closest schema-enum match for this regulatory-framework
chokepoint posture; the schema does not have a regulatory_framework
enum and nation_state_block is the conventional fallback for
state-level licensing / chokepoint regimes (cf. korea-travel-rule-
2022, india-fiu-offshore-vda-block-2023). The honest-note
coverage_gap observation row records the forward-looking,
not-yet-measurable downstream UA-VASP cascade with
attribution=unknown per the brief.

Structural contribution to the dataset: a wartime-context S4
nation-state regulatory-framework event positioned alongside the
Korea Travel Rule 2022 (FATF R.16 national implementation) and the
India FIU offshore-VDA block 2023 (FIU-IND show-cause + MEITY URL
blocking) as comparable_main_2017_present national VASP-regulation
events. Distinguishes itself by (a) wartime-context enabling
function (legalization-as-defensive-financial-policy), (b)
dual-regulator architecture (NSSMC + NBU), and (c) dispersed
cascade across 2022-2024 secondary rulemaking rather than a single
point-in-time enforcement action. Related events:
eu-tfr-recast-2023 (supranational sibling at the EU-27 level) and
fatf-r15-vasp-travel-rule-2019 (supranational parent of the
VASP-licensing regime concept).

censorship precedent. EveryDNS (then the dominant free-DNS
provider, serving ~500k domains) invoked a TOS interference clause

ancestor of all three: a corporate intermediary at the
domain-resolution layer terminating service under TOS in response
to pressure that the intermediary itself frames as
infrastructure-stability rather than legal compulsion. Paired with
the sibling wikileaks-amazon-aws-eviction-2010-12 (hosting-layer
termination 2010-12-01), the two events constitute the
foundational pre-crypto reference cascade for the cross-layer
intermediary-termination pattern this corpus documents at the
